findings.claim: The objective says a type argument such as List<String> turns a run-time ClassCastException into a compile-time error. Parameterized types enable stronger compile-time checking in type-safe code, but they do not categorically convert every possible ClassCastException: raw/unchecked operations, heap pollution, and non-reifiable generic arrays can still produce ClassCastException at run time.

evidence.section: Introducing Generics — stronger type checks at compile time, elimination of casts, and Raw Types
JLS 4.10.2 and 4.12.2 — unchecked operations and heap-pollution example ending in run-time ClassCastException

findings.recommendation: Narrow o2 to observable, correct behavior, for example: “Explain how List<String> lets the compiler reject adding a non-String in type-safe generic code and removes the read-side cast, while raw or unchecked code can still fail at run time.” Carry the qualification into the page and checks.

findings.claim: The objective attributes a HashSet/HashMap bug to changing any key field after insertion. Java specifies the hazard only when the mutation affects equals comparisons (and, for a hash key, its equality/hashCode state); changing an unrelated mutable field does not by itself break lookup.

evidence.section: Map interface — mutable keys: behavior is unspecified when a changed value affects equals comparisons

findings.recommendation: Change o3 to say “changing fields that participate in equals/hashCode while the key is stored.” Use examples that contrast an identity-affecting mutation with an unrelated-field mutation.

findings.claim: The objective asks whether “a List, a Set or a Map” keeps insertion or sorted order without naming an implementation. Set and Map interfaces do not promise one universal encounter order; implementations differ, HashMap has no order guarantee, and Set.of iteration order is unspecified. The prediction is therefore under-specified unless each scenario names the implementation.

evidence.section: Set interface — Unmodifiable Sets: iteration order is unspecified and subject to change
Map interface — encounter-order guarantees vary by implementation; TreeMap guarantees order while HashMap does not

findings.recommendation: Name concrete implementations in o1 and every prediction scenario (for example ArrayList, HashSet, LinkedHashSet, HashMap, LinkedHashMap, TreeMap), and separately test duplicate semantics from encounter/sorted order.

findings.claim: The frozen sources support ResultSet iteration and Java Stream mechanics, but none of the sources assigned to this topic grounds the database-side half of deciding where filtering and aggregation belongs. This leaves an important SQL-versus-in-memory tradeoff objective without the required live first-party evidence for the target PostgreSQL curriculum.

evidence.section: PostgreSQL 18 §7.2 Table Expressions — WHERE, GROUP BY, and HAVING form the SQL row-processing pipeline
PostgreSQL 18 §2.7 Aggregate Functions — aggregate calculations and the WHERE-before-aggregate rule

findings.recommendation: Add version-pinned official PostgreSQL filtering/grouping evidence to the source snapshot (or explicitly bind to equivalent frozen sql-jdbc-foundations evidence) before authoring. State a bounded decision rule and examples rather than an unsupported blanket performance slogan.
